h1: Entry Exit System: what UK travellers need to know
intro: The EU’s Entry Exit System (EES) has replaced passport stamps for British travellers visiting most of Europe. The first time you cross a Schengen border under the new system, you give your fingerprints and a photo, and it can mean long queues at busy times. Here’s how the Entry Exit System works, who it applies to, how it affects children and UK residents on other passports, and how to get through the border with less stress this Christmas and beyond.

sections.heading: What is the Entry Exit System?
sections.text:
The Entry/Exit System is the EU’s digital border record for non-EU travellers on short stays. It started on 12 October 2025 and has been fully running across the Schengen area since 10 April 2026. Instead of stamping your passport, border officers now record your passport details, your entry and exit dates, a photo of your face and your fingerprints.

The system also counts your days automatically, so it knows exactly how long you’ve spent in the Schengen area. That makes the 90 days in any 180 days rule much easier to enforce.

sections.heading: Who has to register?
sections.text:
Everyone travelling to the Schengen area on a short stay without EU residence rights goes through EES, including:
- British passport holders on holiday, visiting family or travelling for business
- UK residents on other passports, such as Indian, Pakistani, Nigerian or Chinese passports, who travel on a Schengen visa
- Children of all ages, although under-12s aren’t fingerprinted

You don’t need to register: if you’re an EU citizen, if you’re a British national with an EU residence document (such as a Withdrawal Agreement residence card), if you hold certain other EU residence permits or long-stay visas, or if you’re Irish. UK and EU dual citizens travelling on their EU passport are also exempt. If you’re exempt, show your document to the border officer rather than registering.

sections.heading: Which countries use the Entry Exit System?
sections.text:
EES applies when you enter or leave any of the 29 Schengen countries, including France, Spain, Italy, Portugal, Greece, Germany, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Norway.

It doesn’t apply to Ireland or Cyprus, because neither is in the Schengen area.

sections.heading: What happens at the border
sections.text:
The first time you enter the Schengen area under EES, an officer or a self-service kiosk will scan your passport, take a photo and take four fingerprints. You may be asked where you’re staying, how long you’ll be there and whether you have enough money for your trip, so keep your return ticket and accommodation details handy.

Your record lasts three years. On later trips in that time you usually only need a quick face or fingerprint check, which should be faster. You may also be asked for a fingerprint or photo when you leave.

If you travel from Dover, Eurotunnel Folkestone or Eurostar at St Pancras, the French checks happen before you leave the UK. Dover and Folkestone have dedicated EES areas, and Eurostar may ask you to use kiosks before the ticket gates. If you fly, or take a ferry from another port, you register on arrival in Europe.

sections.heading: Children and the Entry Exit System
sections.text: Children under 12 don’t give fingerprints, but they still have their photo taken and get their own EES record. Every child needs their own passport, and families with young children are usually processed at a staffed desk rather than a kiosk, as children can’t use the self-service machines.

sections.heading: How to get through the queues
sections.text:
Queues have been long at some airports, especially at peak times such as school holidays. To make things easier:
- Allow extra time, both when you arrive in Europe and before your flight home
- Follow the advice from your airline, ferry or rail operator about arrival times
- Check your passport is in date and meets the rules for your destination before you book
- Keep a printout or screenshot of your accommodation and return travel
- Keep track of your days if you travel often, so you stay within 90 days in any 180

Overstaying is now recorded automatically, and it can lead to fines or problems on future trips.

sections.heading: EES isn’t a visa, and it isn’t ETIAS
sections.text:
EES is free and you don’t apply for it in advance. It’s simply how your border crossing is recorded. Ignore any website asking you to pay for EES.

It’s also separate from ETIAS, the EU’s planned online travel authorisation for British visitors. ETIAS hasn’t started yet and no launch date has been announced. Read our guide to [ETIAS for UK travellers](/blog/etias-for-uk-travellers/) for the latest.

If you live in the UK on a passport that needs a Schengen visa, EES doesn’t replace your visa. You still need the visa in your passport before you travel, and you’ll be registered in EES at the border as well.

faqs.q: Do I need to pay for the Entry Exit System?
faqs.a: No. EES is free and there’s nothing to apply for. Any website charging for EES is not official.

faqs.q: Do British children have to register in EES?
faqs.a: Yes. Children have their photo taken and get their own record, but under-12s don’t give fingerprints.

faqs.q: Does EES apply when I travel to Ireland or Cyprus?
faqs.a: No. Ireland and Cyprus aren’t in the Schengen area, so EES doesn’t apply there.

faqs.q: How long does my EES registration last?
faqs.a: Your record lasts three years, so later trips in that time should usually be quicker.

faqs.q: I live in the UK on an Indian passport. Does EES replace my Schengen visa?
faqs.a: No. You still need a valid Schengen visa before you travel. You’ll also be registered in EES at the border.
